objectives.objective: Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives
keyPoints: Precision comes from applicable decision rules, not from asking for care: "flag only when the claimed behaviour contradicts actual code behaviour" beats "check that comments are accurate".
"Be conservative" and "only high-confidence findings" define nothing the model can apply.
Model self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated — it is often most confident in its false positives.
Make criteria categorical: name the issue types to report (bugs, security flaws) and the ones to skip (style preferences, established local patterns).
Anchor each severity level with explicit criteria plus concrete code examples so classification is matching, not mood.
objectives.watchFor: False positives spend developer trust faster than true positives earn it — disable a noisy category while you fix its criteria rather than letting it discredit the accurate ones.

question.stem: A CI review agent flags style nits alongside real bugs, and developers have started ignoring all of its comments. What is the most effective change?
options: Instruct the agent to be conservative and report only high-confidence findings
Define explicit categories to flag (bugs, security flaws) and to skip (style preferences, established local patterns), with severity criteria anchored by code examples
Filter findings by the agent's self-reported confidence score
Reduce the number of findings reported per pull request to the top three
question.answerWhy: Precision comes from categorical rules the model can apply identically on every run, including severity criteria anchored to concrete examples. "Be conservative" defines nothing, confidence filtering relies on a poorly calibrated signal that is often highest on false positives, and capping the count discards real findings without improving what qualifies as one.

objectives.objective: Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality
keyPoints: Few-shot is the strongest lever when detailed instructions still produce inconsistent output — it fixes both format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix) and judgment.
Target 2–4 examples at the ambiguous scenarios, each showing why one action beat a plausible alternative, so the reasoning generalizes.
For false-positive reduction, pair examples: an acceptable pattern beside a genuine issue, with the rationale for each.
For extraction, demonstrate varied document structures (inline citations vs bibliographies, narrative prose vs structured schedules) to fix format-driven misses.
Examples teach conventions for approximate or unusual source language.
objectives.watchFor: Enumerating dozens of examples turns few-shot into lookup — and only choosing obvious examples wastes the mechanism, since the value is in the ambiguous cases.

question.stem: An extraction pipeline returns null for a publication-date field on documents where the date appears in a bibliography rather than a header, even though it is present. What fixes it best?
options: Mark the field required so the model must populate it
Add a few targeted examples demonstrating correct extraction from the structural variants that are failing, including bibliography-style sources
Add a stricter instruction stating that the date is always present somewhere in the document
Retry the extraction until a non-null value is returned
question.answerWhy: The misses are driven by unfamiliar document structure, and a handful of examples covering those variants teaches the model where to look in each layout. Making the field required or insisting the value exists pressures the model into fabricating a date, and retrying reproduces the same structural blind spot.

objectives.objective: Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas
keyPoints: Define an extraction tool whose input parameters are your target schema and read data from the tool_use response — this makes structure structural, not probabilistic.
It eliminates syntax errors only; semantically wrong values (line items that don't sum, swapped fields) are still schema-valid.
tool_choice: "auto" allows plain text (the source of intermittent parser breakage); "any" guarantees a tool call while the model picks the schema; forced selection pins one specific tool.
Use "any" when several extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown; force a tool when a specific step must run first.
Make fields optional/nullable when sources may lack them, and give enums honest exits — "unclear" for ambiguity, "other" plus detail for novelty.
objectives.watchFor: Forcing a specific tool when the document type is unknown corrupts every document that does not match the forced schema.

question.stem: An extraction pipeline handles invoices, contracts, and reports, each with its own schema, and the document type is unknown at request time. Occasional plain-text responses break the parser. What tool_choice setting fits?
options: "auto", with a prompt instruction to always call a tool
"any", so a tool call is guaranteed while the model selects the matching schema
Forced selection of the invoice extraction tool as the most common case
"auto", with a validation step that reprompts when plain text is returned
question.answerWhy: "any" is exactly the middle rung needed here: conversational text becomes impossible while the model retains the choice of which schema applies. "auto" leaves the plain-text path open regardless of prompt wording or a reprompt patch, and forcing one tool misapplies the invoice schema to every contract and report.

objectives.objective: Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality
keyPoints: Validate semantics — schema validation plus business rules — because tool use eliminates only syntax errors.
Retry with error feedback: send the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation errors; blind identical retries mostly reproduce the failure.
Know when retries cannot succeed: information absent from the source is not a format error — fix it upstream or make the field nullable.
Extract both stated and calculated values and flag disagreement; surface internal inconsistencies with a conflict flag rather than resolving them silently.
Instrument findings with the triggering construct (a detected_pattern field) so dismissals and false positives are analyzable.
objectives.watchFor: Pushing harder on retries for absent information wastes budget at best and teaches the model to fabricate plausible values at worst.

question.stem: An invoice extraction fails validation because the line items do not sum to the stated total. What is the correct handling?
options: Retry the identical request until an extraction that reconciles is returned
Retry with the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error — and extract both stated and calculated totals, flagging the disagreement
Silently replace the stated total with the calculated sum before storing the record
Mark the total field optional so the validation no longer fails
question.answerWhy: Feedback-carrying retries let the model see what was wrong and correct misplaced or misread values, and capturing both the stated and calculated totals surfaces a genuine source conflict instead of hiding it. Blind retries reproduce the same failure, silently overwriting the stated total destroys evidence of a real discrepancy, and loosening the schema suppresses the signal entirely.

keyPoints: The Batches API trades latency for cost: ~50% savings, a processing window of up to 24 hours, and no latency SLA.
Fits non-blocking latency-tolerant work (overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation); disqualifies blocking workflows like pre-merge checks.
Batch requests do not support multi-turn tool calling — agentic loops must run synchronously or be restructured as single-turn requests with pre-collected context.
Every request carries a custom_id: on partial failure, resubmit only the failed items, modified to fix the cause (e.g. chunking oversized documents).
SLA arithmetic: submission cadence plus the 24-hour window sets worst-case delivery — submitting every 4 hours bounds completion at 28 hours.
objectives.watchFor: "Usually fast" is not an SLA — never build deadlines on observed batch latency, and never submit a corpus with an unvalidated prompt when a sample would have taught the same lesson cheaply.

question.stem: A team proposes moving their pre-merge review checks to the Message Batches API for the 50% discount. What is the sound assessment?
options: Reject it — pre-merge checks are blocking, and the processing window extends to 24 hours with no latency SLA
Accept it, since batch turnaround is usually a few minutes in practice
Accept it, provided failed items are resubmitted by custom_id
Accept it for large pull requests only, keeping small ones synchronous
question.answerWhy: Batch is for latency-tolerant work, and a developer blocked on a merge cannot wait inside a window that may run to 24 hours with no guarantee. Observed turnaround is not a contract, and neither failure-recovery hygiene nor splitting by pull-request size changes the fact that the workflow is blocking.

objectives.objective: Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures
keyPoints: Self-review is structurally limited: a session that generated the code retains its generation reasoning and rationalizes rather than questions.
The fix is a second independent instance that receives the code without the generator's reasoning context.
Single-pass review of large changesets suffers attention dilution — detailed early feedback, cursory later notes, and contradictory findings across files.
Multi-pass architecture: per-file passes for local issues plus a separate integration pass for cross-file data flow.
Calibrated confidence (measured against outcomes, not self-reported in the moment) can route review attention.
objectives.watchFor: Larger context windows change what fits, not how evenly it is analyzed — and cross-run consensus filters suppress intermittently caught real bugs while stable false judgments survive.

question.stem: A team's review step runs in the same session that generated the code and passes over a 40-file changeset in one go. Findings are shallow and sometimes contradictory. What architecture fixes this?
options: Enable extended thinking and add adversarial framing to the review prompt
An independent Claude instance that receives the code without generation context, running per-file passes plus a separate cross-file integration pass
A larger context window so the whole changeset is analyzed at once
Three review runs, reporting only findings that appear in at least two of them
question.answerWhy: Two separate defects are in play — self-review bias and attention dilution — and they need instance isolation plus a multi-pass split respectively. Extended thinking deliberates longer inside the same blind spot, a bigger window changes capacity rather than evenness of attention, and consensus filtering discards intermittently detected real defects.
